population.note: FICTIONAL. ~262M US adults × 16% ≈ 42M current users. Arithmetic: 22% ever − 16% current = 6% of adults (~16M) who used and are off now. Of the 22 points of ever-users, ~13 have stopped at least once (consistent with ~1/3 one-year persistence among starters, softened by orals and Medicare's $50 copay); ~7 of those 13 restarted (54% cumulative over a multi-year window, above the 36–47% within-one-year figure) and are among today's current users. Current 16 = ~9 never-stopped + ~7 restarters; cycled_off_and_on = 7/22 ≈ 32%. Age-weighted check (adult shares 20/33/24/23%): 0.2×8 + 0.33×14 + 0.24×26 + 0.23×16 ≈ 16.1. 65+ nearly doubles (9→16) because Medicare made the Bridge permanent; the bottom income third climbs fastest (Medicaid opt-ins in 30 states + DC) but stays below the national rate, because 20 states, most of them Southern, never opted in and that is where obesity is highest. About 4M current users (~10%) have a BMI under 27 and take low-dose oral drugs for 'metabolic health'. They are concentrated in the top third, cash-pay or gray market. Pediatric: ~0.7% of under-18s, mostly adolescents 12–17 on Medicaid (EPSDT) or commercial plans; prescribing to 8–11s is still specialist-only and affluent-skewed. Off-drug populations: ~16M ex-users, many in regain; ~20M adults with obesity who have never been covered (non-opt-in Medicaid states, employers that dropped coverage, the uninsured).

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the GLP-1 Bridge pilot was converted into a permanent Part D obesity benefit from Jan 2028. Medicare pays a negotiated $229/month (down from $245; the IRA negotiated semaglutide price of $274 took effect Jan 2027), and the beneficiary copay stays $50. Medicaid: 30 states + DC opted into the CMS obesity-drug model at the same $229. Payer mix of ~42M users: Medicare 9.6M (5.0M diabetes, 4.6M obesity), Medicaid 5.4M (2.2M diabetes, 3.2M obesity), TRICARE/VA 1.0M. Public total 16.0M (38%), the largest single payer. Commercial 13.5M (32%), cash direct/TrumpRx 9.5M (23%), gray market 3.0M (7%). Medicare obesity spend: 4.6M × $229 × 12 ≈ $12.6B gross, minus copays (4.6M × $50 × 12 ≈ $2.8B) ≈ $9.9B/yr net. Medicaid obesity: 3.2M × $229 × 12 ≈ $8.8B/yr, of which ~68% federal ≈ $6.0B. CBO rescored the permanent Medicare benefit at ~$96B over 2028–2037 (≈ $9.9B/yr rising with enrolment, less ~$10B of modelled offsets in hospital and diabetes spending), up from the ≥$35B 2026–2034 score for the pilot.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 60+ generic semaglutide brands at $6–40/month, with exports to ~100 countries. Canada: generic semaglutide at CAD 70–110/month, now also sold to US buyers through cross-border telepharmacies. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and Egypt have generics. Generic oral semaglutide is launching in India in 2028. Tirzepatide is still under patent almost everywhere. US exclusivity runs to roughly 2031–32.
access.note: Managed decline: TrumpRx and manufacturer-direct cash prices for injectables are $199–299/month, oral starter doses $149, maintenance orals $199–249. The Wegovy list price of $1,349 is unchanged and almost nobody pays it. Orals are ~58% of new starts and ~44% of all fills, so injectables still hold a slim majority of volume through tirzepatide and long-term injectors. Employer coverage for weight management fell from 60% to 52% as employers pointed members to Medicare-anchored cash prices. The gray market regrew after the 503B exclusion was finalised (Jun 2027). ~3M users buy imported Indian/Canadian generic semaglutide through 'personal importation' telehealth, or 'research peptide' retatrutide and cagrilintide from Chinese and Indian synthesisers, at $40–120/month. FDA import alerts and warning letters slow it but have not contained it.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg, label updated for non-inferiority to injectable Wegovy; Rybelsus)
GLP-1/amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Dec 2026)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Apr 2028)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in obesity (tirzepatide, 2027)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: low-dose 'metabolic health' / longevity use by people without obesity: ~4M users, mostly orforglipron or oral semaglutide through cash telehealth memberships ($129–199/month) or the gray market
alcohol reduction: supplemental filings for alcohol use disorder are under FDA review and not approved; widely prescribed off-label
nicotine and compulsive-behaviour reduction, including by military and occupational-health clinicians
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: Oral parity is realised through an existing product in a new form, not a new molecule. A 72-week head-to-head trial (reported Mar 2027) showed oral semaglutide 25 mg non-inferior to weekly injectable Wegovy 2.4 mg (~15–16% each), and FDA updated the label. No pill yet matches tirzepatide (~21%) or retatrutide. CagriSema was approved Dec 2026 against placebo; it has a modest share after losing to tirzepatide. Retatrutide: BLA filed Feb 2027, approved Apr 2028 (14 months later, priority voucher), with dysesthesia labelled. It was sold as gray-market 'research peptide' for two years before approval. Amycretin is still in phase 3, with no filing. Survodutide filed Sep 2028, decision 2029+. MariTide (monthly) and oral amycretin are not on the US market. Bimagrumab-type muscle adjuncts are in phase 3.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common effect and the leading cause of stopping. It is somewhat lower with slow oral titration and higher with retatrutide.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; Ozempic 'not recommended in severe gastroparesis' (Jan 2025) stands.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss; visible in retatrutide's label.
No new causal evidence; absolute risk low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; multidistrict litigation ongoing, no verdicts.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~25–30% of weight lost is lean mass. Concern has widened to normal-weight longevity users and Medicare-age adults now covered in large numbers.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No regulation. Geriatric societies advise resistance training and protein; CMS's Part D benefit materials recommend strength programmes, not required.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict; no new signal.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; still no US class label.
FDA's Jan 2026 removal of the warning stands.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', apathy)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Acknowledged as uncommon. Post-marketing surveys and clinic registries suggest roughly 1–3% of users report clinically meaningful apathy or decreased interest, often dose-related and reversible on dose reduction. This is no new effect, only the existing one quantified.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The 'apathy/decreased interest' line was added to the postmarketing section of retatrutide's and Foundayo's labels (2028). Obesity-medicine clinics added a screening question at dose escalation.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still conflicting between trial and real-world data. Larger cohorts settle around half to two-thirds of lost weight regained within 12–18 months.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; underpins chronic-therapy coverage design in Medicare.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: More case reports in older Medicare users and low-dose wellness users eating very little; no causal quantification.
Known from phase 3 and labelled at approval; mostly mild. Also reported among pre-approval gray-market users.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents who may take these for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~6 years of RCT follow-up now. No signal, and still no data on decades of use or on the ~32% of ever-users who cycle.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on new approvals; NIH-funded cycling cohort launched 2027.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / gray-market product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FDA adverse-event reports tied to compounded or imported product passed ~3,400 by mid-2028. Wrong-concentration 'research peptide' retatrutide is the fastest-growing category.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion finalised Jun 2027; import alerts on Indian and Chinese peptide suppliers; warning-letter waves continue.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~30% of US households. Snack, confectionery and sugary-drink volumes are down another 3–5%, partly offset by price. 'GLP-1 friendly' high-protein and small-format SKUs are now ordinary shelf categories, not a niche. Pharma-adjacent nutrition partnerships (Nestlé, Abbott, Conagra) target Medicare members. The JPMorgan $30–55B by 2030 range is holding, nearer the low end so far.

alcohol.state: US spirits and beer volumes are down ~3% a year. Heavy drinkers, the top 10% of drinkers and ~60% of sales, are the most likely to be on-drug and to cut back. Premium 'occasion' pours and non-alcoholic lines grow but do not offset the loss. Brown-Forman and Constellation have cut workforce and US capacity.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat. Smaller-plate menus, protein bowls and 'half portion' pricing are standard at chains. Buffets and all-you-can-eat formats are closing in Sun Belt suburbs. Bar revenue at casual dining is soft.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists are still shrinking: store closures at Torrid and DXL, offset by new 'transition sizing' and rental. Mainstream retailers flatten size curves toward the middle. The backlash supports a small boom in independent plus-size labels.

fitness.state: Strength training and 'GLP-1 companion' programmes are growing, helped by military and police readiness contracts and Medicare Advantage strength benefits. Cardio-centric boutiques are losing share.

insurance.state: Commercial plans are retreating (employer coverage 52%), with BMI ≥35 or comorbidity thresholds and step-through-oral requirements. Public programmes absorb ~38% of users. Medicare Advantage plans compete on GLP-1 'wraparound' benefits. Commercial pharmacy trend has eased to ~8% as orals and negotiated prices bite.

pharma.state: The Lilly/Novo duopoly persists in the US with retatrutide and CagriSema added, and Lilly is ahead. Volume is up ~45% over two years while net price per month falls 15–25%. Revenue is growing more slowly than 2026 forecasts. Ex-US revenue is under generic pressure, and both firms lobby against cross-border importation.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Among affluent and middle-aged people, a lean body reads as maintained, either by medication or by refusing it, and both are now positions. Normal-weight professionals on low-dose 'metabolic' oral drugs make thinness signal access rather than discipline.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Medicare and Medicaid opt-ins have narrowed the gap at the top and bottom of the age range, but the class split moved to geography and choice. The 20 non-opt-in states, mostly Southern, have the highest obesity and the lowest uptake. The affluent use low-dose drugs for longevity; the working poor in non-opt-in states pay cash or buy gray. Visible fatness is increasingly read as either poverty or politics.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals shrink without disappearing. Family-style and 'small plates' are the default, and church potlucks and Thanksgiving have become sites of quiet negotiation. In the backlash, eating heartily is itself a declaration: 'real food' suppers, fasting-as-discipline churches.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Profiles list 'on/off/never' the way they once listed drinking. Some couples report mismatch when one partner is on-drug and stops drinking; the libido complaint is known but uncommon. Fat-positive dating communities have grown visibly in Atlanta, Brooklyn and Portland.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is a dial for one half of the culture and a birthright for the other. The backlash is a coalition: a revived fat-acceptance movement led largely by Black women organisers in Atlanta and online, MAHA-aligned 'natural' parents suspicious of pharma, and evangelical congregations in Texas and Tennessee framing hunger as spiritual discipline, not a disorder. Its members agree on little except that appetite should not be prescribed away. Tennessee and Oklahoma passed laws in 2028 requiring six months of documented lifestyle counselling before prescribing to minors.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Acknowledged as uncommon, ~1–3% clinically meaningful in post-marketing surveys and clinic registries. It is dose-related and usually reverses with dose reduction or stopping. It is now in two labels' postmarketing sections and in clinic screening questions. Most users report nothing of the kind; some report the opposite, relief from 'noise'.
interior_life.framing: Side effect, named and managed like dry mouth on an antidepressant. Separately, the same mechanism is framed as treatment in alcohol-use-disorder filings and occupational nicotine programmes. Backlash rhetoric calls it 'the flattening', far beyond its measured prevalence.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Occupational-health programmes for police, shift workers and the military value reduced snacking, drinking and nicotine. Some departments informally attribute fewer DUIs and less overtime-related weight gain to them, with no rigorous data. A small number of users report lost drive and leave sales or creative jobs. Employers do not track it, and HR guidance treats it like any medical side effect.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: There is a minor literary and musical genre about the 'quiet' (essays, an indie album cycle) and a counter-genre celebrating appetite. Bars and food media court the 'occasion eater'. Intense-flavour products (sour, spicy, bitter) remain popular among users, though not exclusively.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: A recognised but uncommon complaint. Couples therapists add it to intake. Some users lower their dose before anniversaries or holidays, a widely shared practice.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measurable change in political engagement. The side effect is a rhetorical asset for the backlash ('they want you docile'), especially around the military programme, and it surfaces in 2028 primary messaging, though it moves few votes.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access on price and approvals: priority vouchers, the permanent Medicare benefit, the oral label update. Enforcement-heavy on compounding and imports but losing ground to offshore telehealth. HHS is internally split: pro-access CMS and FDA leadership against a MAHA-aligned faction that funds 'lifestyle-first' messaging.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. The permanent Medicare Part D obesity benefit at $229 with a $50 copay; a Medicaid opt-in model in 30 states + DC at the same rate; TrumpRx cash channel at $149–299. TRICARE has restored weight-management coverage for active duty.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Coverage is conditioned on BMI/comorbidity and, increasingly, on 'step through oral' rules. Military and some police programmes tie enrolment to body-composition testing and fitness standards. Enrolment is voluntary, but body-fat failures now come with a pharmacotherapy option attached. Unit medical readiness dashboards record participation, which civil-liberties groups contest.
state.workforce_or_military: DoD 'Metabolic Readiness' initiative (Nov 2027): TRICARE covers incretins for active-duty members over body-fat standards, with ~41,000 enrolled (~3% of 1.3M active duty). Army accession waivers let recruits treated during the Future Soldier Prep Course enlist if they are off-drug and stable by ship date. FAA guidance clarifies that pilots on stable doses may fly after an observation period. Police departments in Houston, Phoenix and Columbus and two large hospital systems run night-shift programmes through their health plans.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The US–India price gap ($229–299 vs $6–40) is a live political issue. Cross-border telepharmacy from Canada and India is tolerated in practice while illegal in principle. Lilly and Novo trade US manufacturing investment for tariff relief. China supplies most gray-market peptide API.

events.event: Head-to-head trial finds oral Wegovy 25 mg non-inferior to weekly injectable Wegovy at 72 weeks; FDA updates label and Medicare plans begin requiring an oral trial first

FDA finalises exclusion of semaglutide/tirzepatide/liraglutide from 503B compounding; telehealth sellers pivot to 'personal importation' of Indian and Canadian generics and to research-peptide retatrutide; FDA import alert follows in October

CMS makes the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge a permanent Part D obesity benefit from January 2028 at $229/month with a $50 copay; 30 states and DC join a Medicaid opt-in at the same price; CBO scores ~$96B over ten years

Pentagon launches 'Metabolic Readiness': TRICARE restores GLP-1 coverage for active-duty members over body-fat standards; Army allows recruits treated in prep courses to enlist; FAA clarifies pilot rules

Survey finds ~4M Americans without obesity take low-dose oral GLP-1s for 'metabolic health'; Hims & Hers, Function Health and Ro market longevity memberships at $129–199/month, legal as off-label prescription
'Enough' rally in Nashville draws fat-acceptance organisers, MAHA parents and evangelical pastors; Tennessee and Oklahoma enact six-month lifestyle-first rules before prescribing to minors

open_tensions: Public programmes are now the default payer, but 20 non-opt-in states with the highest obesity rates are left out. The drug follows the Medicaid map, and the 2028 election makes that map political.

The gray market supplies the people coverage excludes and the wellness users regulators never intended, including with next-generation molecules before or outside approval. Enforcement is pushing them offshore, not off-drug.

Readiness programmes make the drug part of institutional fitness for soldiers, police and shift workers. Enrolment is voluntary on paper, while unit dashboards and the backlash's 'docility' rhetoric argue over what voluntary means.
Normal-weight longevity users, Medicare-age users at risk of losing muscle, and adolescents now in Medicaid are all on a drug with ~6 years of follow-up and no data on decades of use or on cycling.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide in the US; brand exclusivity runs to roughly 2031–32.
Wegovy's list price is still $1,349/month, and almost nobody pays it.
The Medicare beneficiary copay for obesity GLP-1s is still $50/month, first set by the GLP-1 Bridge pilot.
Foundayo (orforglipron) is still sold as a daily oral small molecule, with oral starter doses at $149 through TrumpRx and manufacturer-direct channels.
The FDA's January 2026 removal of the suicidal-ideation warning from Saxenda, Wegovy and Zepbound stands; suicidal ideation remains debunked.

prose.headline: The Pill Won, Medicare Pays, the Army Wants You Lean — and Nashville Says Enough: America at 16 Percent
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028, about one American adult in six takes an incretin drug: roughly forty-two million people. Another sixteen million have taken one and stopped, and a third of everyone who has ever started has stopped and come back at least once. The drug is no longer new. It is a payer category, a line on a dating profile and a political position.

The needle stopped mattering in the spring of 2027. A head-to-head trial showed the Wegovy pill doing what the weekly Wegovy shot does, about fifteen or sixteen percent of body weight. The FDA rewrote the label, and Medicare plans began asking patients to try the pill first. Today most new starts swallow rather than inject, though people chasing the larger losses of tirzepatide, or of retatrutide, approved in April, still use pens. No pill matches those yet.

The bigger change is who pays. CMS made the Medicare Bridge pilot permanent in January: $229 a month to the manufacturer, fifty dollars to the beneficiary. Thirty states and the District joined a Medicaid model at the same price. Public programmes now cover about sixteen million users, more than any other kind of payer. Employers kept retreating, and barely half still cover weight management. Their benefits managers send members to cash channels at two or three hundred dollars, because the government has made those prices look reasonable. The price kept falling, but slowly, by negotiation. List price is still $1,349 and no one pays it.

The map is the problem. Mississippi, Alabama, Texas and most of the states with the highest obesity rates did not join the Medicaid model. There, a forty-year-old warehouse worker without employer coverage chooses between a $199 cash pill and a $60 vial of Indian generic semaglutide shipped through a telehealth site that calls itself a personal-importation service. After the FDA closed compounding pharmacies in 2027, the gray market moved overseas and grew. It now supplies perhaps three million Americans, along with research-peptide retatrutide that circulated for two years before approval, sometimes at the wrong concentration.

The gray market also supplies some customers no one planned for. About four million Americans without obesity take low-dose pills for what the memberships call metabolic health. They are lawyers in Austin, founders in Los Angeles, retired surgeons in Scottsdale, paying $149 a month for an off-label prescription or less for something imported. Geriatricians worry about their muscle mass. They don't worry much about anything else, and there is no new safety signal. The apathy some users describe is now in two labels as uncommon, perhaps one or two users in a hundred, and it usually lifts when the dose comes down.

The state has found a use for it. Since November the Pentagon has covered the drugs for active-duty members over body-fat standards, and the Army lets prep-course recruits enlist once they are stable and off it. Houston and Phoenix police unions negotiated it into their plans. Hospital night shifts offer it beside the melatonin.

The backlash is real and local. In May, a rally in Nashville under the word Enough brought together people who rarely share a stage: Atlanta fat-acceptance organisers, MAHA mothers who distrust Lilly, and Tennessee pastors who preach hunger as discipline. Tennessee and Oklahoma now require six months of lifestyle counselling before a minor can be prescribed. Inside the same HHS, CMS expands coverage while another office funds posters about walking.

Snack volumes are down again, beer is down again, and plus-size chains keep closing stores. Nothing collapsed. The restaurants have smaller plates and the gyms sell squats. From most angles the country looks a little thinner and a little quieter, and it is arguing about who that was for.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Linda Pruitt takes the pill at 6:10 with plain water, thirty minutes before coffee, standing at the counter in her robe in Chattanooga. The pharmacy bag on the windowsill says $50.00 in blue pen. She has stopped looking at the bathroom scale.

At nine she drives to Ridgedale Baptist to help set up for Wednesday supper. Carol is already there, slicing pound cake into proper slabs. Carol's pastor preached last month on fasting as obedience, and Carol has been handing out little cards that say ENOUGH. Linda takes one and puts it in her purse beside the pill bottle.

At noon her son Derek calls from his cruiser. The sheriff's office weighed everyone again. He's on the shot now, through the county plan. "It's nothing, Mom. Half the shift's on it." He sounds fine. He sounds the same.

At three her granddaughter Kaylee, fourteen, gets off the bus and eats two packs of sour straws at the kitchen table. Her pediatrician said six months of the counselling first, now that it's the law, and then they'd talk. Kaylee doesn't want to talk. She wants the straws.

At supper Linda takes a quarter slab of Carol's cake and leaves most of it. Carol notices. Neither says anything.

At nine she sits on the porch. Across the street the Hendersons' boy, home from Fort Cavazos, is lifting a kettlebell in the garage light, counting out loud. Linda listens to the count. She used to like a cigarette about now. She doesn't miss it. She tries to remember whether she ever did.
